title: Operating Systems
source_note: LASU CS department curriculum document, CSC205 'Operating System I' course description (OS structures, process model, inter-process communication, mutual exclusion problems, scheduling, and memory management), directly matching the course code and level assigned here.

questions.question: An operating system is best defined as:
options: System software that manages computer hardware and provides services for application programs
A type of application used only for word processing
A physical hardware component inside the CPU
A programming language used to write web pages
questions.correct_answer: System software that manages computer hardware and provides services for application programs
questions.explanation: An operating system is the core system software that manages hardware resources (CPU, memory, devices) and provides a platform on which application software runs.

questions.question: In a monolithic operating system structure, the entire operating system is:
options: Compiled as a single large program where all components can directly call each other
Split into isolated hardware-only modules with no software
Run entirely inside a web browser
Composed of independent virtual machines only
questions.correct_answer: Compiled as a single large program where all components can directly call each other
questions.explanation: A monolithic OS structure implements the entire operating system as one large program running in kernel mode, where internal procedures can call each other freely.

questions.question: In a layered operating system structure, the system is organized as:
options: A hierarchy of layers, each built on top of lower layers and offering services to the layer above
A single undivided block of code
A collection of unrelated applications with no OS control
Only hardware components with no software abstraction
questions.correct_answer: A hierarchy of layers, each built on top of lower layers and offering services to the layer above
questions.explanation: A layered OS design divides the system into layers, where each layer uses the functions of the layer below it, improving modularity and simplifying debugging.

questions.question: A virtual machine operating system structure allows:
options: Multiple isolated instances of an operating environment to run on the same physical hardware
Only one program to run on a computer at any time
Hardware to run without any operating system
Files to be permanently deleted automatically
questions.correct_answer: Multiple isolated instances of an operating environment to run on the same physical hardware
questions.explanation: The virtual machine approach creates an illusion of multiple separate machines on top of shared physical hardware, each capable of running its own operating system.

questions.question: In the client-server model of operating system structure, most OS services are provided by:
options: User-level server processes that communicate with client processes via message passing
A single hardware chip with no software involved
The BIOS exclusively
External printers only
questions.correct_answer: User-level server processes that communicate with client processes via message passing
questions.explanation: The client-server model moves most OS functionality out of the kernel into separate server processes, with clients requesting services via message passing.

questions.question: What is a 'process' in operating systems terminology?
options: A program in execution, along with its current state and resources
A file stored permanently on disk
A piece of computer hardware
A type of network cable
questions.correct_answer: A program in execution, along with its current state and resources
questions.explanation: A process is an instance of a program that is being executed, including its program counter, registers, and the resources allocated to it.

questions.question: Which of the following is typically NOT one of the basic process states?
options: Compiled
Running
Ready
Blocked/Waiting
questions.correct_answer: Compiled
questions.explanation: The basic process states are typically new, ready, running, waiting/blocked, and terminated; 'compiled' describes a stage of program translation, not a process execution state.

questions.question: What information does a Process Control Block (PCB) store?
options: Information about a process such as its state, program counter, registers, and memory allocation
The physical location of the CPU on the motherboard
The content of all files on the hard disk
The list of all installed application software
questions.correct_answer: Information about a process such as its state, program counter, registers, and memory allocation
questions.explanation: The Process Control Block (PCB) is a data structure the OS uses to store all information needed to manage and track a specific process, including its state and register values.

questions.question: What does it mean when a process transitions from 'running' to 'ready' state?
options: The process is preempted or voluntarily gives up the CPU but remains able to run
The process has permanently finished execution
The process has encountered a fatal unrecoverable error
The process has been deleted from memory
questions.correct_answer: The process is preempted or voluntarily gives up the CPU but remains able to run
questions.explanation: A running process moves to the ready state when it is preempted (e.g. by the scheduler) or voluntarily yields the CPU, while still being eligible to run again later.

questions.question: What is a 'race condition' in the context of concurrent processes?
options: A situation where the outcome of execution depends on the unpredictable timing or interleaving of processes accessing shared data
A competition between two computers to boot up first
A method for speeding up CPU clock cycles
A technique for encrypting network traffic
questions.correct_answer: A situation where the outcome of execution depends on the unpredictable timing or interleaving of processes accessing shared data
questions.explanation: A race condition occurs when multiple processes access and manipulate shared data concurrently, and the final outcome depends on the particular, unpredictable order of execution.

questions.question: What is the 'critical section' in concurrent programming?
options: A segment of code where a process accesses shared resources that must not be concurrently accessed by more than one process
The very first line of code in any program
A section of the hard disk reserved for the operating system only
The part of a program that handles user input exclusively
questions.correct_answer: A segment of code where a process accesses shared resources that must not be concurrently accessed by more than one process
questions.explanation: The critical section is the part of a program where shared resources are accessed; only one process should execute in its critical section at a time to avoid race conditions.

questions.question: What does 'mutual exclusion' ensure in concurrent process management?
options: That only one process can execute in its critical section involving a shared resource at any given time
That all processes run at exactly the same speed
That every process has unlimited access to memory
That processes can never communicate with each other
questions.correct_answer: That only one process can execute in its critical section involving a shared resource at any given time
questions.explanation: Mutual exclusion is a property that guarantees only one process at a time can access a shared resource within its critical section, preventing data inconsistency.

questions.question: What is a semaphore used for in operating systems?
options: A synchronization tool used to control access to shared resources by multiple processes
A device used to physically connect a monitor to a computer
A tool for compiling source code
A type of file compression algorithm
questions.correct_answer: A synchronization tool used to control access to shared resources by multiple processes
questions.explanation: A semaphore is a synchronization primitive (an integer variable with atomic wait/signal operations) used to coordinate access to shared resources among concurrent processes.

questions.question: In the producer-consumer problem, what is the main challenge being addressed?
options: Coordinating access to a shared, bounded buffer so producers don't overfill it and consumers don't read from an empty buffer
Determining which process should be terminated first
Encrypting data before it is written to disk
Choosing the fastest programming language for I/O
questions.correct_answer: Coordinating access to a shared, bounded buffer so producers don't overfill it and consumers don't read from an empty buffer
questions.explanation: The producer-consumer problem involves synchronizing producer processes (which add items to a shared buffer) and consumer processes (which remove items), avoiding buffer overflow or underflow.

questions.question: The dining philosophers problem is a classic illustration of which operating system concept?
options: Deadlock and resource allocation among concurrent processes
File compression algorithms
Network routing protocols
Graphical user interface design
questions.correct_answer: Deadlock and resource allocation among concurrent processes
questions.explanation: The dining philosophers problem is a classic synchronization example used to illustrate challenges of deadlock, resource allocation, and starvation among concurrent processes.

questions.question: What is 'deadlock' in operating systems?
options: A situation where two or more processes are each waiting for a resource held by another, so none can proceed
A state where the CPU is turned off
A type of scheduling algorithm that prioritizes short jobs
A method for allocating disk space efficiently
questions.correct_answer: A situation where two or more processes are each waiting for a resource held by another, so none can proceed
questions.explanation: Deadlock occurs when a set of processes are blocked because each process is holding a resource and waiting for another resource held by another process in the set.

questions.question: Which of the following is a necessary condition for deadlock to occur?
options: Circular wait
Unlimited memory
Single-threaded execution only
No shared resources exist
questions.correct_answer: Circular wait
questions.explanation: Circular wait, along with mutual exclusion, hold and wait, and no preemption, is one of the four necessary conditions for a deadlock to occur.

questions.question: What does 'starvation' refer to in process scheduling?
options: A situation where a process is perpetually denied the resources it needs to proceed, often due to scheduling policy bias
A process running out of available RAM entirely
A hardware failure affecting the CPU
The complete shutdown of the operating system
questions.correct_answer: A situation where a process is perpetually denied the resources it needs to proceed, often due to scheduling policy bias
questions.explanation: Starvation occurs when a process is indefinitely delayed or denied necessary resources, often because a scheduling algorithm favors other processes repeatedly.

questions.question: Which CPU scheduling algorithm processes jobs strictly in the order they arrive, without preemption?
options: First-In-First-Out (FIFO/FCFS)
Shortest Job First
Round Robin
Priority Scheduling
questions.correct_answer: First-In-First-Out (FIFO/FCFS)
questions.explanation: First-In-First-Out (FIFO), also called First-Come-First-Served (FCFS), schedules processes strictly in the order they arrive in the ready queue, with no preemption.

questions.question: In Round Robin scheduling, each process is given:
options: A fixed small unit of CPU time (time quantum) before being moved to the back of the ready queue
Unlimited CPU time until it finishes execution
No CPU time at all
Priority based only on its file size
questions.correct_answer: A fixed small unit of CPU time (time quantum) before being moved to the back of the ready queue
questions.explanation: Round Robin scheduling allocates a fixed time quantum to each process in turn; if the process does not finish within that time, it is preempted and moved to the back of the ready queue.

questions.question: Which scheduling algorithm selects the process with the smallest estimated execution time next?
options: Shortest Job First (SJF)
Round Robin
First-In-First-Out
Highest Response Ratio Next only
questions.correct_answer: Shortest Job First (SJF)
questions.explanation: Shortest Job First (SJF) scheduling selects the waiting process with the smallest estimated run time to execute next, minimizing average waiting time under ideal conditions.

questions.question: What distinguishes preemptive scheduling from non-preemptive scheduling?
options: Preemptive scheduling allows a running process to be interrupted and moved to ready state, while non-preemptive does not
Non-preemptive scheduling always runs faster than preemptive scheduling
Preemptive scheduling can only be used with a single process
There is no real difference between the two approaches
questions.correct_answer: Preemptive scheduling allows a running process to be interrupted and moved to ready state, while non-preemptive does not
questions.explanation: In preemptive scheduling, the operating system can forcibly suspend a running process to allocate the CPU elsewhere; in non-preemptive scheduling, a process keeps the CPU until it voluntarily releases it.

questions.question: What is a common scheduling criterion used to evaluate CPU scheduling algorithms?
options: Average waiting time
The color of the monitor
The brand of the hard disk
The number of installed fonts
questions.correct_answer: Average waiting time
questions.explanation: Average waiting time (along with turnaround time, throughput, and CPU utilization) is a key metric used to evaluate the effectiveness of CPU scheduling algorithms.

questions.question: In real memory management, what does the 'single-user contiguous scheme' mean?
options: The entire main memory (aside from OS space) is allocated to a single running program at a time
Multiple users can run programs simultaneously in separate memory blocks
Memory is divided into equal fixed partitions for many users
Memory is never allocated to any program
questions.correct_answer: The entire main memory (aside from OS space) is allocated to a single running program at a time
questions.explanation: In the single-user contiguous memory scheme, one program occupies the available memory space (besides the OS) at any given time, a simple early memory management approach.

questions.question: In fixed partition memory management, main memory is divided into:
options: A predetermined number of partitions of fixed size, each holding one process
An infinite number of variable-sized partitions
A single partition shared by all processes simultaneously
Partitions that grow automatically without limit
questions.correct_answer: A predetermined number of partitions of fixed size, each holding one process
questions.explanation: Fixed partitioning divides memory into a set number of partitions of predetermined (fixed) size at system startup, with each partition holding one process.

questions.question: What is 'virtual memory' in an operating system?
options: A memory management technique that gives programs the illusion of a large, continuous address space by using disk storage to extend physical RAM
A type of memory that exists only in cloud storage
Memory that is not real and cannot store any data
A memory chip that never loses data even after being physically destroyed
questions.correct_answer: A memory management technique that gives programs the illusion of a large, continuous address space by using disk storage to extend physical RAM
questions.explanation: Virtual memory allows the OS to use disk space to simulate additional RAM, giving processes the illusion of a large, contiguous address space even if physical memory is limited.

questions.question: In paged memory allocation, memory is divided into:
options: Fixed-size blocks called pages (in logical memory) and frames (in physical memory)
Variable-size blocks that change every clock cycle
A single block equal to the size of the entire hard disk
Blocks defined only by file extension
questions.correct_answer: Fixed-size blocks called pages (in logical memory) and frames (in physical memory)
questions.explanation: Paging divides a process's logical memory into fixed-size pages and physical memory into equally sized frames, allowing non-contiguous allocation of memory to a process.

questions.question: What does a 'page replacement policy' determine in virtual memory management?
options: Which page currently in memory should be swapped out to make room for a new page being brought in
How many users can log into the system at once
The physical color scheme of the desktop
The list of installed printer drivers
questions.correct_answer: Which page currently in memory should be swapped out to make room for a new page being brought in
questions.explanation: When a new page must be loaded into a full memory, a page replacement policy (such as LRU or FIFO) decides which existing page to evict to make space.

questions.question: What does 'demand paging' mean in virtual memory systems?
options: Pages are loaded into memory only when they are actually referenced/needed during execution
All pages of a program are loaded into memory before execution begins
Pages are never loaded into memory at all
Only the operating system's pages are ever loaded
questions.correct_answer: Pages are loaded into memory only when they are actually referenced/needed during execution
questions.explanation: Demand paging loads a page into physical memory only when a process actually references it, rather than loading the entire program into memory upfront, saving memory resources.

questions.question: What is a 'nucleus' (or kernel) in the context of process implementation within an operating system?
options: The core part of the operating system responsible for managing processes, memory, and hardware at the lowest level
A hardware chip that stores only the BIOS
An external application used for word processing
A type of computer virus
questions.correct_answer: The core part of the operating system responsible for managing processes, memory, and hardware at the lowest level
questions.explanation: The nucleus, or kernel, is the central component of an operating system that directly manages hardware resources, processes, and low-level system operations.

questions.question: What distinguishes 'job scheduling' from 'process scheduling' in operating systems?
options: Job scheduling selects which jobs are admitted into the system for processing, while process scheduling selects which ready process runs on the CPU next
Job scheduling and process scheduling are exactly the same operation
Process scheduling determines which files can be deleted
Job scheduling only applies to network requests
questions.correct_answer: Job scheduling selects which jobs are admitted into the system for processing, while process scheduling selects which ready process runs on the CPU next
questions.explanation: Job scheduling (long-term scheduling) decides which jobs are brought into the system to become processes, while process scheduling (short-term scheduling) decides which ready process gets the CPU next.

questions.question: What is the main purpose of an interrupt in process handling within an operating system?
options: To signal the CPU to temporarily suspend the current process and handle an event such as I/O completion
To permanently terminate all running processes
To format the hard disk automatically
To install new application software
questions.correct_answer: To signal the CPU to temporarily suspend the current process and handle an event such as I/O completion
questions.explanation: Interrupts allow hardware or software events (like I/O completion) to signal the CPU, causing it to suspend the current process temporarily and handle the event via an interrupt handler.
